 1. Make the balls half their current sizes.
 2. Make the headline explanatory text way shorter, we only need to explain the very core, not everything.
 3. Make the two balls colliding to blink brighter colors, independent on who's colliding with whom and their speeds.

- deep-review: Multi-agent code review of a PR, branch, commit, or local changes through six lenses calibrated for the MonoDreams engine. Catches framework-fit problems, system-ordering bugs, missed downstream callers, ECS-purity violations, and premises that no test protects.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	# physics — premises
2	
3	> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the physics module:
4	> `RigidBodyComponent`, `VelocityComponent`, `GravitySystem`, and
5	> `VelocitySystem`. Read this before changing any of those pieces or any
6	> system that writes velocity / reads `Transform.Delta` for movement.
7	
8	## `GravitySystem` affects only entities with `RigidBodyComponent` + `VelocityComponent`
9	
10	`GravitySystem` queries on entities that have both `RigidBodyComponent`
11	(with gravity active) and `VelocityComponent`. Missing either component
12	means gravity does not apply.
13	
14	**Why:** gravity needs both a participant flag (`RigidBodyComponent.Gravity`)
15	and a target field to write to (`VelocityComponent.Current`). Falling back
16	to defaults would hide configuration bugs where a dev expected gravity
17	but never added the required components.
18	**Breaks:** a "floating" entity that was supposed to fall sits still;
19	the dev assumes gravity is broken, when in fact one of the two
20	components is missing.
21	**Tests:**
22	`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/InfiniteRunnerTests.cs::PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`
23	exercises this integration indirectly (player has both components and
24	falls as expected).
25	**Depends on:** —
26	
27	## `VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of physics entities
28	
29	Game systems should express motion as writes to `VelocityComponent.Current`;
30	`VelocitySystem` applies that velocity to `TransformComponent.Position`
31	each frame. Game systems should not mutate `TransformComponent.Position`
32	directly on physics entities.
33	
34	**Why:** writing to `VelocityComponent` is what makes
35	`TransformComponent.Delta` meaningful for swept collision and what feeds
36	the resolution systems' impulse computations. Direct position mutation
37	bypasses both.
38	**Breaks:** entities teleport instead of move — swept collision sees no
39	`Delta` and misses contacts; resolution can't reverse the move because
40	the impulse history is wrong.
41	**Tests:** none yet (indirectly exercised by `InfiniteRunnerTests`).
42	**Depends on:** collision — "Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`".
43	
44	## `RigidBodyComponent.FreezePositionX/Y` and `FreezeRotation` are honored by resolution
45	
46	The resolution systems read the freeze flags and zero out the
47	corresponding correction. Movement systems that mutate a frozen axis
48	directly will desync from resolution, because resolution will keep
49	reverting it.
50	
51	**Why:** freeze flags are the single source of truth for "this axis
52	doesn't move." Splitting that authority between game code and the
53	flag produces inconsistent behavior depending on which system ran last.
54	**Breaks:** a game system pushes a frozen entity along the frozen
55	axis; resolution un-pushes it; the entity vibrates or stays put with
56	wasted CPU.
57	**Tests:** none yet.
58	**Depends on:** —
59	
60	## `VelocityComponent.Delta` is `Current - Last`, updated by `VelocitySystem`
61	
62	`VelocityComponent.Delta` reports the change between the current and
63	previous velocity. `VelocitySystem` updates `Last` from `Current` at the
64	end of its pass. Systems reading `Delta` get the previous frame's
65	effective velocity change.
66	
67	**Why:** `Delta` is useful for impulse-based behaviors (a character
68	that reacts to its own deceleration, dampening systems that fade
69	energy). The "end of pass" update keeps `Delta` meaningful for the
70	next frame regardless of what else writes to `Current` mid-frame.
71	**Breaks:** code that reads `Delta` before `VelocitySystem` runs sees
72	last frame's value; code that reads after sees zero (or whatever fresh
73	zero-update produces). Both are valid mid-frame; the bug is reading
74	without understanding which side of the update you're on.
75	**Tests:** none yet.
76	**Depends on:** —
77	
78	## `RigidBodyComponent.IsKinematic` selects the resolution path
79	
80	`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` is the lighter, kinematic-style
81	response (move-and-stop without mass effects).
82	`TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem` is the mass- and
83	velocity-aware response. Which resolution system an entity is subject to
84	is determined by **which resolution systems the screen registers**, not
85	by the `RigidBodyComponent` flag alone.
86	
87	**Why:** consistent with ECS purity — systems don't dispatch on entity
88	state, they query and act. The flag is a hint to the screen which
89	resolution system to register for the relevant entity stack.
90	**Breaks:** a dev sets `IsKinematic = false` expecting a physical
91	response, but the screen only registers the kinematic resolution
92	system; the entity behaves kinematically anyway.
93	**Tests:** none yet.
94	**Depends on:** —
95	
96	## Known limitations (acknowledged gaps)
97	
98	- **No high-speed velocity cap** — there is no built-in clamp on
99	  `VelocityComponent.Current` to prevent tunneling regardless of gameplay
100	  velocity. Gameplay code is responsible for not exceeding reasonable
101	  speed-to-collider-size ratios. *Velocity-cap safety net is on the
102	  backlog.*
103	
104	## Open questions
105	
106	- **`RigidBodyComponent.Gravity` factor field** — confirmed semantic:
107	  per-entity gravity scaling. Heavier multipliers fall faster, lighter
108	  multipliers float. Not yet captured as a premise — promote when more
109	  gameplay code uses it.
110	- **`RigidBodyComponent.Mass`** — used by
111	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem` today. Nothing prevents
112	  other systems from reading it for mass-dependent gameplay (push
113	  strength, AI weight class). Acknowledged: usage may expand.
114	
115	## Aspirational direction
116	
117	- Velocity-cap safety net to prevent tunneling at extreme speeds.
118	- Broader use of `RigidBodyComponent.Mass` in gameplay-facing systems
119	  (knockback, push, AI weight classes).
120	
121	## Follow-up debt
122	
123	The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:
124	
125	- `GravitySystem` affects only entities with `RigidBodyComponent` +
126	  `VelocityComponent` *(indirectly exercised by
127	  `InfiniteRunnerTests.PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`)*
128	- `VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of physics entities
129	- `RigidBodyComponent.FreezePositionX/Y` and `FreezeRotation` are
130	  honored by resolution
131	- `VelocityComponent.Delta` is `Current - Last`, updated by `VelocitySystem`
132	- `RigidBodyComponent.IsKinematic` selects the resolution path

# physics — premises

> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the physics module:
> `RigidBodyComponent`, `VelocityComponent`, `GravitySystem`, and
> `VelocitySystem`. Read this before changing any of those pieces or any
> system that writes velocity / reads `Transform.Delta` for movement.

## `GravitySystem` affects only entities with `RigidBodyComponent` + `VelocityComponent`

`GravitySystem` queries on entities that have both `RigidBodyComponent`
(with gravity active) and `VelocityComponent`. Missing either component
means gravity does not apply.

**Why:** gravity needs both a participant flag (`RigidBodyComponent.Gravity`)
and a target field to write to (`VelocityComponent.Current`). Falling back
to defaults would hide configuration bugs where a dev expected gravity
but never added the required components.
**Breaks:** a "floating" entity that was supposed to fall sits still;
the dev assumes gravity is broken, when in fact one of the two
components is missing.
**Tests:**
`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/InfiniteRunnerTests.cs::PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`
exercises this integration indirectly (player has both components and
falls as expected).
**Depends on:** —

## `VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of physics entities

Game systems should express motion as writes to `VelocityComponent.Current`;
`VelocitySystem` applies that velocity to `TransformComponent.Position`
each frame. Game systems should not mutate `TransformComponent.Position`
directly on physics entities.

**Why:** writing to `VelocityComponent` is what makes
`TransformComponent.Delta` meaningful for swept collision and what feeds
the resolution systems' impulse computations. Direct position mutation
bypasses both.
**Breaks:** entities teleport instead of move — swept collision sees no
`Delta` and misses contacts; resolution can't reverse the move because
the impulse history is wrong.
**Tests:** none yet (indirectly exercised by `InfiniteRunnerTests`).
**Depends on:** collision — "Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`".

## `RigidBodyComponent.FreezePositionX/Y` and `FreezeRotation` are honored by resolution

The resolution systems read the freeze flags and zero out the
corresponding correction. Movement systems that mutate a frozen axis
directly will desync from resolution, because resolution will keep
reverting it.

**Why:** freeze flags are the single source of truth for "this axis
doesn't move." Splitting that authority between game code and the
flag produces inconsistent behavior depending on which system ran last.
**Breaks:** a game system pushes a frozen entity along the frozen
axis; resolution un-pushes it; the entity vibrates or stays put with
wasted CPU.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `VelocityComponent.Delta` is `Current - Last`, updated by `VelocitySystem`

`VelocityComponent.Delta` reports the change between the current and
previous velocity. `VelocitySystem` updates `Last` from `Current` at the
end of its pass. Systems reading `Delta` get the previous frame's
effective velocity change.

**Why:** `Delta` is useful for impulse-based behaviors (a character
that reacts to its own deceleration, dampening systems that fade
energy). The "end of pass" update keeps `Delta` meaningful for the
next frame regardless of what else writes to `Current` mid-frame.
**Breaks:** code that reads `Delta` before `VelocitySystem` runs sees
last frame's value; code that reads after sees zero (or whatever fresh
zero-update produces). Both are valid mid-frame; the bug is reading
without understanding which side of the update you're on.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `RigidBodyComponent.IsKinematic` selects the resolution path

`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` is the lighter, kinematic-style
response (move-and-stop without mass effects).
`TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem` is the mass- and
velocity-aware response. Which resolution system an entity is subject to
is determined by **which resolution systems the screen registers**, not
by the `RigidBodyComponent` flag alone.

**Why:** consistent with ECS purity — systems don't dispatch on entity
state, they query and act. The flag is a hint to the screen which
resolution system to register for the relevant entity stack.
**Breaks:** a dev sets `IsKinematic = false` expecting a physical
response, but the screen only registers the kinematic resolution
system; the entity behaves kinematically anyway.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Known limitations (acknowledged gaps)

- **No high-speed velocity cap** — there is no built-in clamp on
  `VelocityComponent.Current` to prevent tunneling regardless of gameplay
  velocity. Gameplay code is responsible for not exceeding reasonable
  speed-to-collider-size ratios. *Velocity-cap safety net is on the
  backlog.*

## Open questions

- **`RigidBodyComponent.Gravity` factor field** — confirmed semantic:
  per-entity gravity scaling. Heavier multipliers fall faster, lighter
  multipliers float. Not yet captured as a premise — promote when more
  gameplay code uses it.
- **`RigidBodyComponent.Mass`** — used by
  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem` today. Nothing prevents
  other systems from reading it for mass-dependent gameplay (push
  strength, AI weight class). Acknowledged: usage may expand.

## Aspirational direction

- Velocity-cap safety net to prevent tunneling at extreme speeds.
- Broader use of `RigidBodyComponent.Mass` in gameplay-facing systems
  (knockback, push, AI weight classes).

## Follow-up debt

The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:

- `GravitySystem` affects only entities with `RigidBodyComponent` +
  `VelocityComponent` *(indirectly exercised by
  `InfiniteRunnerTests.PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`)*
- `VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of physics entities
- `RigidBodyComponent.FreezePositionX/Y` and `FreezeRotation` are
  honored by resolution
- `VelocityComponent.Delta` is `Current - Last`, updated by `VelocitySystem`
- `RigidBodyComponent.IsKinematic` selects the resolution path

1	# MonoDreams — Core Tenets
2	
3	> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
4	> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
5	> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
6	> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.
7	
8	## 1. Framework, not library
9	
10	MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
11	the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
12	the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
13	embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
14	low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
15	(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).
16	
17	**Two users, equal weight.**
18	- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
19	  play primitives.
20	- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
21	  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
22	  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.
23	
24	**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
25	general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
26	than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
27	hiding inside the framework.
28	
29	## 2. ECS purity & composition
30	
31	The architecture is composition all the way down:
32	
33	- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
34	  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
35	  logic belongs in a system.
36	- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
37	  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
38	  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
39	  run after.
40	- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
41	  their own.
42	- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
43	  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
44	  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
45	  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
46	  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.
47	
48	**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
49	more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
50	are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
51	should always have more systems than components.
52	
53	**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
54	search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
55	creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
56	this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
57	of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
58	reusable.
59	
60	**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
61	systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
62	Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
63	dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
64	name alone.
65	
66	**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
67	system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
68	just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
69	generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
70	isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.
71	
72	### Aspirational direction
73	
74	- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
75	  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
76	  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
77	  enforce or warn at registration time.
78	- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
79	  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
80	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
81	  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
82	  closest prototype.
83	- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
84	  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
85	  works and signals that it's maintained.
86	
87	## 3. Hierarchy & Transform
88	
89	`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
90	rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
91	matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
92	properties that walk the parent chain.
93	
94	**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
95	project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
96	trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
97	`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
98	operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
99	collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
100	specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
101	consumers too.
102	
103	**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
104	link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
105	structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
106	split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
107	panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
108	move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
109	`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
110	backlog** (§9); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
111	is consolidated.
112	
113	**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
114	descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
115	re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
116	the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
117	pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.
118	
119	**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
120	two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
121	`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
122	prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
123	"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
124	consistency" (§9). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
125	(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
126	assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.
127	
128	### Aspirational direction
129	
130	Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
131	directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
132	operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
133	swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
134	currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
135	reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.
136	
137	## 4. Rendering pipeline
138	
139	The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
140	here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
141	than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:
142	
143	**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
144	There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
145	one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
146	Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
147	`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
148	(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
149	**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
150	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
151	the pipeline.
152	
153	**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
154	code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
155	parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.
156	
157	**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
158	the prep-cull-sort-render module goes at the end. The recommended order
159	inside the module, from the reference assembly
160	(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
161	`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
162	→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.
163	
164	**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
165	- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
166	- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
167	- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
168	
169	The `Visible` tag is added and removed by `CullingSystem` based on the
170	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and
171	HUD entities don't need `Visible`; if you put a `Visible`-gated entity
172	on UI by mistake, it will always render (which is usually the desired
173	outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
174	entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the
175	pipeline, and the dev stares at an invisible sprite). The renderable
176	entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
177	DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.
178	**This split is a known wart** (§9): `Visible` may become a property of
179	`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.
180	
181	**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth`, in this
182	order: `SpritePrepSystem` initializes it from the sprite's layer,
183	`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
184	`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
185	minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
186	to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
187	fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
188	flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.
189	
190	**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual resolution
191	(immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom, position, and
192	rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
193	multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
194	fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
195	register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
196	whatever the `Camera` reports.
197	
198	## 5. Physics & collision
199	
200	The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
201	collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
202	detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
203	game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
204	gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.
205	
206	**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
207	(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
208	kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags; `BoxCollider` carries an AABB
209	and active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries model-space vertices,
210	world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
211	is auto-applied to any entity with a collider component so detection
212	queries can match a unified tag.
213	
214	**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
215	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
216	**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
217	Each stage owns one job:
218	- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
219	- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
220	- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
221	  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
222	- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
223	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
224	  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
225	- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
226	  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
227	
228	Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
229	reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
230	ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
231	through walls — see §3.
232	
233	**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
234	the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
235	filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
236	broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
237	that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
238	broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.
239	
240	**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
241	holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
242	thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
243	contexts.
244	
245	**One collider of each type per entity.** Today the framework assumes
246	an entity has at most one `BoxCollider` and at most one `ConvexCollider`.
247	This is implicit, not enforced. Multiple colliders of the same type on
248	a single entity is undefined behavior — if you need it, that's a
249	framework change, not a workaround.
250	
251	### Aspirational direction
252	
253	Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
254	end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.
255	
256	## 6. Level loading & entity spawning
257	
258	Levels live in `.ldtk` files (LDtk editor) and `.json` exports from
259	Blender (`Tools/blender_level_export.py`). The pipeline is identical
260	in shape: a request loads a file, a parser walks the data, and the
261	parser emits `EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into
262	entities.
263	
264	**The pipeline.**
265	1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
266	2. **Two systems subscribe to the message directly** —
267	   `LevelLoadRequestSystem` (LDtk path) and `BlenderLevelParserSystem`
268	   (Blender path). Each gates on the level identifier (see the
269	   `Blender_` prefix note below).
270	3. `LevelLoadRequestSystem` loads the LDtk file and **adds
271	   `CurrentLevelComponent` to the world**; the LDtk parsers
272	   (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`) then **subscribe
273	   to `CurrentLevelComponent` being added** and parse on add.
274	   `BlenderLevelParserSystem`, in contrast, parses directly from the
275	   message — an asymmetry that's a known wart (see "Aspirational
276	   direction" below and the per-module premises).
277	4. Parsers emit `EntitySpawnRequest`s.
278	5. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
279	   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.
280	
281	**Key invariant — the LDtk parsers react to component lifecycle, not
282	to push messages.** Their pattern (subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
283	added) is the engine-wide *intended* default. A test or tool that adds
284	`CurrentLevelComponent` manually triggers them just as well as the
285	regular `LoadLevelRequest` path. The Blender parser predates the
286	pattern and remains message-driven; harmonizing it is on the backlog
287	(§9). For new parsers, follow the LDtk pattern — resist the urge to
288	make a system "only respond when the right message arrived" — that's
289	coupling the system to an upstream sequence that should be the
290	assembler's choice.
291	
292	**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
293	`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
294	setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
295	warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
296	throw** — this is on the backlog (§9). For now, treat the warning as a
297	high-severity signal during development.
298	
299	**`Blender_` identifier prefix.** Both `LevelLoadRequestSystem` (LDtk)
300	and `BlenderLevelParserSystem` (Blender) subscribe to `LoadLevelRequest`
301	independently. The Blender parser filters by the `Blender_` prefix and
302	handles the load when matched; `LevelLoadRequestSystem` unconditionally
303	attempts the LDtk path, fails for Blender-prefixed names, and removes
304	`CurrentLevelComponent` to clean up. **This dual-subscribe dispatch by
305	name prefix is a quick hack** (§9); a content-driven dispatch (a format
306	field in the level data) is the eventual replacement.
307	
308	## 7. The reference pipeline
309	
310	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
311	assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
312	overall order, end-to-end:
313	
314	1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
315	   under replay.
316	2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
317	   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
318	   dialogue state).
319	3. **Physics module** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
320	   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
321	   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
322	   `TransformCommitSystem`.
323	4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
324	   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
325	5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
326	6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
327	7. **Render module** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
328	   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
329	   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.
330	
331	Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
332	recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
333	non-physics screens skip the physics module, UI-only screens may have
334	no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
335	input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
336	ahead of culling.
337	
338	### Aspirational direction
339	
340	A declarative system-dependencies API would let
341	`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
342	me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
343	exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
344	skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
345	tests.
346	
347	## 8. Debug & testing
348	
349	The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
350	*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.
351	
352	**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
353	`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
354	once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
355	`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
356	[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
357	environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
358	screenshots) for test isolation.
359	
360	**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
361	directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
362	time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
363	skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
364	auto-exits when the replay finishes.
365	
366	**Screenshots.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2 seconds to
367	the debug directory. Off by default; enable by setting `"screenshots":
368	true` in `input_replay.json`.
369	
370	**Headless mode — two hosts, two contracts.** There are two headless
371	paths and they do *not* do the same thing:
372	
373	- **Examples** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`)
374	  creates a 1×1 off-screen window and **early-returns from `Draw`** — it
375	  runs Update-side logic at max speed but renders **nothing**. It is
376	  convenient for fast logic/replay integration tests via `GameTestRunner`
377	  but cannot observe any visual or render-path behaviour. Treat it as the
378	  logic-only path; don't rely on it for rendering correctness.
379	- **Demos** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Demos -- --headless --screen
380	  <name> --frames <N> --exit`) is the **observe-and-self-verify** path
381	  (issue #28). It keeps a real `GraphicsDevice` on a hidden, full-virtual-
382	  resolution backbuffer, **renders every frame** (`Draw` is not a no-op),
383	  dumps non-blank PNGs to `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`, logs periodic live-heap
384	  samples, and self-terminates after `<N>` frames. This is the supported
385	  way for an agent to verify its own work on the demo host without a human.
386	  See the `debug` module premises ("Headless Demos renders every frame";
387	  "Headless heap samples measure the live set") and
388	  `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`.
389	
390	A literal zero-window mode / null `GraphicsDevice` is **not** possible on
391	MonoGame DesktopGL 3.8.4 (the window hosts the GL context); a hidden
392	window that never presents is the achievable form of "headless render".
393	
394	**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
395	`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
396	debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
397	exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
398	`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
399	today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
400	(parsing), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).
401	
402	**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
403	("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
404	yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
405	field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.
406	
407	## 9. Refactor backlog (named cruft)
408	
409	Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
410	Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
411	will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
412	code".
413	
414	- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
415	  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
416	  reasoning about hierarchy.
417	- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
418	  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
419	  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
420	- **`Blender_` identifier prefix** (§6). Dispatch by name prefix is a
421	  hack; a content-driven dispatch (format field in level data) is the
422	  eventual replacement.
423	- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
424	  Intended behaviour is to throw.
425	- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
426	  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
427	  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
428	- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
429	  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
430	  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
431	  contract.
432	- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
433	  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
434	  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
435	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
436	- **Examples headless mode is logic-only** (§8). Its `Draw` early-returns,
437	  so it renders nothing — fine for replay/logic tests, useless for visual
438	  observation. The Demos headless path (issue #28) is the load-bearing
439	  observe-and-self-verify route and *does* render; the remaining debt is
440	  that the Examples mode is still named "headless" despite not rendering,
441	  and the two paths could eventually share one host abstraction.
442	- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
443	  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
444	- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
445	  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
446	  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
447	- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
448	  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
449	  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
450	  contract should ship with at least one usage.

# MonoDreams — Core Tenets

> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.

## 1. Framework, not library

MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).

**Two users, equal weight.**
- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
  play primitives.
- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.

**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
hiding inside the framework.

## 2. ECS purity & composition

The architecture is composition all the way down:

- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
  logic belongs in a system.
- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
  run after.
- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
  their own.
- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.

**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
should always have more systems than components.

**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
reusable.

**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
name alone.

**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.

### Aspirational direction

- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
  enforce or warn at registration time.
- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
  closest prototype.
- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
  works and signals that it's maintained.

## 3. Hierarchy & Transform

`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
properties that walk the parent chain.

**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
consumers too.

**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
backlog** (§9); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
is consolidated.

**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.

**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
consistency" (§9). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.

### Aspirational direction

Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.

## 4. Rendering pipeline

The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:

**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
the pipeline.

**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.

**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
the prep-cull-sort-render module goes at the end. The recommended order
inside the module, from the reference assembly
(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.

**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.

The `Visible` tag is added and removed by `CullingSystem` based on the
camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and
HUD entities don't need `Visible`; if you put a `Visible`-gated entity
on UI by mistake, it will always render (which is usually the desired
outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the
pipeline, and the dev stares at an invisible sprite). The renderable
entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.
**This split is a known wart** (§9): `Visible` may become a property of
`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.

**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth`, in this
order: `SpritePrepSystem` initializes it from the sprite's layer,
`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.

**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual resolution
(immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom, position, and
rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
whatever the `Camera` reports.

## 5. Physics & collision

The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.

**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags; `BoxCollider` carries an AABB
and active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries model-space vertices,
world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
is auto-applied to any entity with a collider component so detection
queries can match a unified tag.

**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
Each stage owns one job:
- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.

Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
through walls — see §3.

**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.

**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
contexts.

**One collider of each type per entity.** Today the framework assumes
an entity has at most one `BoxCollider` and at most one `ConvexCollider`.
This is implicit, not enforced. Multiple colliders of the same type on
a single entity is undefined behavior — if you need it, that's a
framework change, not a workaround.

### Aspirational direction

Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.

## 6. Level loading & entity spawning

Levels live in `.ldtk` files (LDtk editor) and `.json` exports from
Blender (`Tools/blender_level_export.py`). The pipeline is identical
in shape: a request loads a file, a parser walks the data, and the
parser emits `EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into
entities.

**The pipeline.**
1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
2. **Two systems subscribe to the message directly** —
   `LevelLoadRequestSystem` (LDtk path) and `BlenderLevelParserSystem`
   (Blender path). Each gates on the level identifier (see the
   `Blender_` prefix note below).
3. `LevelLoadRequestSystem` loads the LDtk file and **adds
   `CurrentLevelComponent` to the world**; the LDtk parsers
   (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`) then **subscribe
   to `CurrentLevelComponent` being added** and parse on add.
   `BlenderLevelParserSystem`, in contrast, parses directly from the
   message — an asymmetry that's a known wart (see "Aspirational
   direction" below and the per-module premises).
4. Parsers emit `EntitySpawnRequest`s.
5. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.

**Key invariant — the LDtk parsers react to component lifecycle, not
to push messages.** Their pattern (subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
added) is the engine-wide *intended* default. A test or tool that adds
`CurrentLevelComponent` manually triggers them just as well as the
regular `LoadLevelRequest` path. The Blender parser predates the
pattern and remains message-driven; harmonizing it is on the backlog
(§9). For new parsers, follow the LDtk pattern — resist the urge to
make a system "only respond when the right message arrived" — that's
coupling the system to an upstream sequence that should be the
assembler's choice.

**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
throw** — this is on the backlog (§9). For now, treat the warning as a
high-severity signal during development.

**`Blender_` identifier prefix.** Both `LevelLoadRequestSystem` (LDtk)
and `BlenderLevelParserSystem` (Blender) subscribe to `LoadLevelRequest`
independently. The Blender parser filters by the `Blender_` prefix and
handles the load when matched; `LevelLoadRequestSystem` unconditionally
attempts the LDtk path, fails for Blender-prefixed names, and removes
`CurrentLevelComponent` to clean up. **This dual-subscribe dispatch by
name prefix is a quick hack** (§9); a content-driven dispatch (a format
field in the level data) is the eventual replacement.

## 7. The reference pipeline

`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
overall order, end-to-end:

1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
   under replay.
2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
   dialogue state).
3. **Physics module** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
   `TransformCommitSystem`.
4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
7. **Render module** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.

Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
non-physics screens skip the physics module, UI-only screens may have
no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
ahead of culling.

### Aspirational direction

A declarative system-dependencies API would let
`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
tests.

## 8. Debug & testing

The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.

**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
screenshots) for test isolation.

**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
auto-exits when the replay finishes.

**Screenshots.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2 seconds to
the debug directory. Off by default; enable by setting `"screenshots":
true` in `input_replay.json`.

**Headless mode — two hosts, two contracts.** There are two headless
paths and they do *not* do the same thing:

- **Examples** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`)
  creates a 1×1 off-screen window and **early-returns from `Draw`** — it
  runs Update-side logic at max speed but renders **nothing**. It is
  convenient for fast logic/replay integration tests via `GameTestRunner`
  but cannot observe any visual or render-path behaviour. Treat it as the
  logic-only path; don't rely on it for rendering correctness.
- **Demos** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Demos -- --headless --screen
  <name> --frames <N> --exit`) is the **observe-and-self-verify** path
  (issue #28). It keeps a real `GraphicsDevice` on a hidden, full-virtual-
  resolution backbuffer, **renders every frame** (`Draw` is not a no-op),
  dumps non-blank PNGs to `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`, logs periodic live-heap
  samples, and self-terminates after `<N>` frames. This is the supported
  way for an agent to verify its own work on the demo host without a human.
  See the `debug` module premises ("Headless Demos renders every frame";
  "Headless heap samples measure the live set") and
  `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`.

A literal zero-window mode / null `GraphicsDevice` is **not** possible on
MonoGame DesktopGL 3.8.4 (the window hosts the GL context); a hidden
window that never presents is the achievable form of "headless render".

**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
(parsing), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).

**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.

## 9. Refactor backlog (named cruft)

Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
code".

- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
  reasoning about hierarchy.
- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
- **`Blender_` identifier prefix** (§6). Dispatch by name prefix is a
  hack; a content-driven dispatch (format field in level data) is the
  eventual replacement.
- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
  Intended behaviour is to throw.
- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
  contract.
- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
- **Examples headless mode is logic-only** (§8). Its `Draw` early-returns,
  so it renders nothing — fine for replay/logic tests, useless for visual
  observation. The Demos headless path (issue #28) is the load-bearing
  observe-and-self-verify route and *does* render; the remaining debt is
  that the Examples mode is still named "headless" despite not rendering,
  and the two paths could eventually share one host abstraction.
- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
  contract should ship with at least one usage.

5	/// Character classes a <see cref="TextInputComponent"/> accepts. Masking is the
6	/// one "smart" feature this primitive ships with on purpose — richer behaviors
7	/// (formatting, placeholder text, validation / error states) are intentionally
8	/// left out so they can be layered on later without reworking the core.
9	public enum TextInputMask
10	{
11	    /// Accept any printable character the key map produces.
12	    None,
13	    /// Accept only digits 0-9.
14	    Numeric,
15	}
16	
17	/// A minimal editable text field. Pure data: <see cref="TextInputSystem"/> appends
18	/// or deletes characters (honoring <see cref="Mask"/> and <see cref="MaxLength"/>)
19	/// while <see cref="Focused"/> is true, and mirrors <see cref="Text"/> onto the
20	/// linked <see cref="TextEntity"/>'s <c>DynamicTextComponent</c>. Focus itself is
21	/// game-owned — set it from your own click / interaction system, the same way
22	/// button click dispatch is game-owned (see the ui premises).
23	public struct TextInputComponent
24	{
25	    /// Current value. Null is treated as empty.
26	    public string Text;
27	    /// Maximum character count; 0 or less means unbounded.
28	    public int MaxLength;
29	    /// Which characters typing will accept.
30	    public TextInputMask Mask;
31	    /// When true, this field consumes the keyboard this frame.
32	    public bool Focused;
33	    /// The entity whose <c>DynamicTextComponent.TextContent</c> displays <see cref="Text"/>.
34	    public Entity TextEntity;
35	}
36	
37	/// Published by <see cref="TextInputSystem"/> on the frame an input's
38	/// <see cref="TextInputComponent.Text"/> changes. Carries the input entity and its
39	/// new value so game code can react (parse a number, run a search, …) without
