content.content:
1	# rendering — premises
2	
3	> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the rendering pipeline:
4	> `DrawComponent`, `SpriteInfoComponent`, `VisibleComponent`, the
5	> `Camera` class, render targets, `CullingSystem`, `SpritePrepSystem`,
6	> `YSortSystem`, `MasterRenderSystem`, `FinalDrawSystem`, plus the mesh
7	> primitives (`IMeshGenerator`, `MeshData`, `MeshPrepSystem`). Read this
8	> before changing any of those pieces or any system that produces draw
9	> data downstream.
10	
11	## `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive
12	
13	A `DrawComponent`'s `Type` is one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or
14	`Mesh`. One render component per renderable entity; an entity that needs
15	two visual types needs two entities (or a new `DrawElementType` that
16	composes both).
17	
18	**Why:** `MasterRenderSystem` switches batch context based on `Type`
19	(`Sprite`/`Text`/`NinePatch` go through `SpriteBatch`, `Mesh` goes
20	through `BasicEffect` triangles). Allowing a single `DrawComponent` to
21	span two types would force every render path through a per-call branch.
22	**Breaks:** game code that sets a `DrawComponent` to one type and then
23	expects sprite + text behavior renders only one of them, with no
24	diagnostic.
25	**Tests:** none yet.
26	**Depends on:** —
27	
28	## `DrawComponent` is the only render component
29	
30	Do not create new draw or render components. Adding a new visual type
31	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork the
32	pipeline.
33	
34	**Why:** a parallel render component would also need a parallel render
35	system, parallel culling treatment, and parallel layer-depth handling —
36	the framework's value comes from there being exactly one path through
37	the pipeline.
38	**Breaks:** the parallel system either skips entities the main path
39	expected (silent invisibility) or competes with it (z-fighting,
40	double-rendering).
41	**Tests:** none yet.
42	**Depends on:** —
43	
44	## `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*
45	
46	All `SpriteBatch` / `BasicEffect` draw calls happen inside
47	`MasterRenderSystem` (back-buffer composition is `FinalDrawSystem`'s job).
48	Game code must not call `SpriteBatch` directly and must not write a second
49	render system. This is about a single *implementation*, not a single
50	*instance*: a screen registers as many `MasterRenderSystem` instances as it
51	has views (see "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass").
52	
53	**Why:** centralizing the draw call lets one well-understood class own the
54	render-target switch, the batch settings, the sort, and the layer-depth
55	contract. A bespoke second renderer fragments all four; N instances of the
56	*same* renderer do not.
57	**Breaks:** a parallel hand-rolled renderer fights over the active
58	`SpriteBatch`, producing flickering frames, dropped draws, or driver-level
59	errors, and bypasses the sort/layer-depth contract.
60	**Tests:** none yet.
61	**Depends on:** —
62	
63	## One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass
64	
65	A `MasterRenderSystem` instance renders exactly one pass: every entity
66	whose `DrawComponent.Target` equals its `source` id, through its optional
67	`camera` (null ⇒ screen-space, identity transform), into its `destination`
68	render target, which it clears to transparent first. The `source == Main`
69	pass additionally filters on `VisibleComponent` (culling); screen-space
70	passes always render. Multiple cameras, minimaps, splitscreen, CCTV, and
71	portal textures are all just additional instances — a minimap is a second
72	instance with `source = Main`, a second camera, and its own target.
73	`FinalDrawSystem` then composites the targets onto the screen.
74	
75	**Why:** decoupling *what* to draw (`source`), *how* (`camera`), and
76	*where* (`destination`) makes a second view a second instance, not a new
77	code path — the framework's general-over-specialized rule. It also removes
78	the old "the camera only applies to the Main-keyed target" coupling.
79	**Breaks:** two instances writing the *same* destination clear each
80	other's work (each clears on entry) — give every pass its own target and
81	let `FinalDrawSystem` overlap them. Expecting a non-Main source to honor
82	culling: only `source == Main` consults `VisibleComponent`.
83	**Tests:** none yet (the multi-pass + minimap path is exercised by the
84	camera demo, `MonoDreams/camera/demo/CameraDemoScreen.cs`).
85	**Depends on:** "A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its
86	destination".
87	
88	## A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination
89	
90	A `MasterRenderSystem` pass derives its mesh `BasicEffect` projection from
91	the *destination* render target's pixel size
92	(`CreateOrthographicOffCenter(0, dest.Width, dest.Height, 0, …)`), and the
93	camera's view transform centers the view at the camera's virtual
94	resolution. For the two to agree, a pass's `camera.VirtualWidth/Height`
95	must equal its destination render target's size. The minimap obeys this by
96	giving its second camera the same virtual resolution as the main camera and
97	a full-virtual-resolution target, then letting `FinalDrawSystem` shrink
98	that target into the on-screen box.
99	
100	**Why:** projection maps destination pixels → NDC; the camera centers world
101	content at `(VirtualWidth/2, VirtualHeight/2)`. A mismatch puts the centered
102	content somewhere other than the target's middle and scales meshes wrongly.
103	Deriving projection from the destination (not the camera) is what lets
104	screen-space passes carry no camera at all.
105	**Breaks:** a camera whose virtual resolution differs from its destination
106	renders off-center and mis-scaled in that pass.
107	**Tests:** none yet.
108	**Depends on:** "`Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable".
109	
110	## `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list
111	
112	`FinalDrawSystem` takes an ordered `RenderLayer` list and draws each
113	target onto the back buffer in order (later = on top). `RenderLayer.Main`
114	/ `UI` / `HUD` are factories for the standard full-frame layers (carrying
115	the viewport-mode-aware destination rect + sampler); `RenderLayer.Overlay`
116	places a target in a sub-rectangle given in HUD virtual coordinates,
117	mapped to the screen the same way the HUD layer is — so an overlay aligns
118	with HUD chrome drawn at those coordinates. The screen owns the list, so it
119	decides which targets exist, their order, and where each lands.
120	
121	**Why:** the compositor is the natural seam for screen layout — overlays
122	(minimap, CCTV), and eventually tiled splitscreen — without touching the
123	renderer. Driving it from an explicit list (rather than a hardcoded
124	Main→UI→HUD sequence) makes those layouts data, not code forks.
125	**Breaks:** omitting a layer silently drops that target from the screen
126	(its render pass still ran and cleared its target — wasted work, blank
127	result). An overlay rect given in screen pixels instead of HUD virtual
128	coords misaligns with HUD chrome under non-1:1 scaling.
129	**Tests:** none yet (exercised by every demo/example screen and the minimap
130	overlay in the camera demo).
131	**Depends on:** —
132	
133	## Renderable entity stack on the Main target
134	
135	An entity is rendered to the Main target only if it has
136	`TransformComponent + SpriteInfoComponent (or text/mesh equivalent) +
137	DrawComponent + VisibleComponent`. Missing `VisibleComponent` means
138	`MasterRenderSystem` skips silently (it includes `.With<VisibleComponent>()`
139	in the Main-target query).
140	
141	**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is the culling output. `CullingSystem` adds
142	it for entities inside the camera frustum and removes it for entities
143	outside, letting `MasterRenderSystem` skip a frustum check per entity.
144	Splitting it from `DrawComponent` is a wart — see Aspirational.
145	**Breaks:** the canonical missed-tag bug — a dev creates an entity with
146	`SpriteInfoComponent + DrawComponent` and stares at an invisible result
147	with no error. Forgetting to register `CullingSystem` in a new screen
148	makes everything Main-target invisible.
149	**Tests:** none yet. *This is the specific bug from the bootstrap
150	interview that motivated writing premises files in the first place.*
151	**Depends on:** "`VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`".
152	
153	## `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`
154	
155	Game code must not add or remove `VisibleComponent` on Main-target
156	entities. It is managed automatically by `CullingSystem` based on the
157	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. UI and HUD entities may set
158	`VisibleComponent` themselves as a one-shot tag, since those targets
159	ignore culling (see "Three render targets, two behaviors").
160	
161	**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is a derived state on the Main target. Manual
162	mutation creates ghost entities (visible but outside the frustum, wasting
163	draw calls) or phantom-invisible entities (inside the frustum but
164	skipped). `CullingSystem` will overwrite the game-set value next frame
165	anyway.
166	**Breaks:** entities flicker in and out as `CullingSystem` overwrites
167	game-set values frame to frame; or the cull check fights game code
168	forever.
169	**Tests:** none yet.
170	**Depends on:** —
171	
172	## Three render targets, two behaviors
173	
174	`RenderTargetID.Main` is camera-transformed and respects culling.
175	`RenderTargetID.UI` and `RenderTargetID.HUD` are screen-space and always
176	render. Only Main consults `VisibleComponent`.
177	
178	**Why:** UI and HUD are always-on-screen by definition. Culling them
179	would mean checking against the *screen* frustum, which is a degenerate
180	case (everything is inside). `MasterRenderSystem` enforces this by only
181	adding `.With<VisibleComponent>()` to the Main-target query.
182	**Breaks:** putting a Main-target entity on UI/HUD by mistake skips
183	camera transforms — the entity renders at its world coordinates,
184	unscaled by zoom. The reverse (UI on Main) gets culled away when the
185	camera moves.
186	**Tests:** none yet.
187	**Depends on:** —
188	
189	## `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp
190	
191	`MasterRenderSystem` opens a separate `SpriteBatch` for sprites and for text so each gets
192	its own `SamplerState`. Sprites (and the mesh path) default to `PointClamp` — crisp
193	nearest-neighbour scaling for pixel art; text defaults to `LinearClamp` — smooth filtering
194	for bitmap fonts drawn at fractional scale. Both defaults are overridable via the
195	`spriteSampler` / `textSampler` constructor parameters. Because Sprite and Text are now
196	distinct batch types, the interleaved renderer flushes + reopens the batch when switching
197	between them; painter's order is preserved because the draw list is already depth-sorted.
198	
199	**Why:** a single global `LinearClamp` blurred up-scaled pixel sprites (e.g. a 16×16
200	indicator drawn at 48×48); a single global `PointClamp` aliases down-scaled bitmap text.
201	Per-type samplers give each its correct filtering. The mesh path already forced `PointClamp`
202	(`ResetGraphicsStateForMeshRendering`), so sprites now match it.
203	**Breaks:** collapsing the Sprite/Text batch split (one sampler for both) forces a single
204	filter and reintroduces either blurry sprites or aliased text. Passing a non-clamp address
205	mode would wrap/tile sprites at their edges.
206	**Tests:** none yet.
207	**Depends on:** —
208	
209	## The draw set is built once per instance, not per frame
210	
211	A `MasterRenderSystem` instance builds its `EntitySet` (for its `source`)
212	lazily once and reuses it for the instance's lifetime; it is disposed in
213	`Dispose`. It must never call `world.GetEntities()...AsSet()` inside the
214	per-frame `Update`.
215	
216	**Why:** DefaultEcs's `AsSet()` registers component/entity lifecycle
217	subscriptions on the `World`, and the World holds those subscription
218	delegates — which reference the `EntitySet` — alive forever. A set
219	created per frame is therefore never garbage-collected. An earlier version
220	built a fresh set every frame, leaking `EntitySet`s every frame, each
221	retaining its matched-entity array. This is the standing ECS-wide rule
222	(every other `AsSet()` in the engine is cached in a field) applied to the
223	renderer. Note that composing N render passes means N cached sets — fine,
224	because each is built once; two passes with the same `source` (e.g. the
225	main world pass and a minimap pass) hold two equivalent sets, a negligible
226	constant cost, not a per-frame leak.
227	**Breaks:** process memory climbs steadily even on a fully static scene
228	(no entities or assets added), as observed in the camera and physics
229	demos. Eventually OOM on a long-running session.
230	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`
231	asserts a flat live heap across 600 frames of the camera demo (now four
232	render passes).
233	**Depends on:** —
234	
235	## Rendering systems run last in the pipeline
236	
237	In any screen's pipeline assembly, the prep / cull / sort / render stage
238	goes at the tail. Logic that mutates renderable state (positions, sprite
239	source rects, text contents, layer depths) must complete before the prep
240	module reads it.
241	
242	**Why:** the prep stage freezes the state of `DrawComponent`s into the
243	draw queue; mutations after the queue is built are silently lost until
244	next frame.
245	**Breaks:** a game system that updates text mid-render-module sees the
246	old text on screen. A movement system after `CullingSystem` updates
247	positions without re-culling — entities pop in or out by one frame.
248	**Tests:** none yet.
249	**Depends on:** —
250	
251	## Layer-depth ownership pipeline
252	
253	`SpritePrepSystem` initializes `DrawComponent.LayerDepth` from
254	`SpriteInfoComponent.LayerDepth`. `YSortSystem` may override it for
255	entities on Y-sorted layers. `MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final
256	value. Game systems writing `LayerDepth` after `YSortSystem` create
257	undefined sort behavior.
258	
259	**Why:** three writers in a defined order produce one final value. A
260	fourth writer in between (or after) breaks the contract.
261	**Breaks:** entities flicker, depth-fight, or render behind/in-front of
262	static elements unexpectedly.
263	**Tests:** none yet.
264	**Depends on:** —
265	
266	## Y-sort tiebreaker is parent-child bias only
267	
268	`YSortSystem` uses a minimal epsilon (`1e-6f` in
269	`MonoDreams/rendering/System/Draw/YSortSystem.cs`) to bias children
270	relative to their parent's final depth, preserving group ordering.
271	Same-layer entities at the same world Y with no parent-child relationship
272	have no further tiebreaker — render order falls through to entity
273	insertion order.
274	
275	**Why:** parent-child bias is the only ambiguity case the framework
276	treats explicitly; "true ties" are rare in practice (entities at the
277	exact same Y on the same layer).
278	**Breaks:** if true ties become common, flicker can appear when
279	insertion order changes (e.g., re-spawn). The fix is a tiebreaker —
280	possibly entity ID — but that's a framework change, not a workaround.
281	**Tests:** none yet.
282	**Depends on:** —
283	
284	## `Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable
285	
286	`Camera.VirtualWidth` and `Camera.VirtualHeight` are readonly properties
287	set in the constructor (the `Camera` class lives at
288	`MonoDreams/rendering/Camera.cs` because it is a hard dependency of the
289	draw stack — `MasterRenderSystem` reads its position, zoom, and view
290	matrix every frame). Only zoom, position, and rotation are mutable on a
291	live `Camera`.
292	
293	**Why:** virtual resolution defines the world-units-per-pixel ratio.
294	Changing it mid-frame would require recomputing every entity's on-screen
295	size and re-running culling.
296	**Breaks:** a system that tries to change resolution at runtime either
297	silently fails (readonly) or, if it bypasses, produces a fractional
298	frame where culling, layout, and rendering disagree.
299	**Tests:** none yet.
300	**Depends on:** —
301	
302	## `IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list
303	
304	All canonical generators (`CircleMeshGenerator`, `LineMeshGenerator`,
305	`RectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`, `FilledRectangleMeshGenerator`,
306	`GradientPathMeshGenerator`, `CompositeMeshGenerator`) return `MeshData`
307	whose indices describe a triangle list — every triple of indices is one
308	triangle. `MasterRenderSystem` invokes `DrawUserIndexedPrimitives` with
309	`PrimitiveType.TriangleList`.
310	
311	**Why:** triangle lists are the lowest common denominator for the
312	`BasicEffect` path. Triangle strips or fans would require per-shape
313	metadata about which primitive type to use, and would multiply the
314	render path's branching.
315	**Breaks:** a custom generator that emits a triangle strip without
316	setting `DrawComponent.PrimitiveType` correctly produces garbled
317	geometry — the renderer interprets the indices as a list and draws
318	random triangles between them.
319	**Tests:** none yet.
320	**Depends on:** —
321	
322	## `MeshPrepSystem` writes the world matrix once per frame
323	
324	`MeshPrepSystem` reads `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix` and writes it
325	into `DrawComponent.WorldMatrix` for every entity with `Type = Mesh`.
326	This must happen after `HierarchySystem` propagates dirty flags and
327	before `MasterRenderSystem` reads the matrix to bind it to
328	`BasicEffect.World`.
329	
330	**Why:** meshes render in world space — their vertex positions are
331	the geometry's local-space layout, and the world matrix transforms
332	them to where the entity is. Reading `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix`
333	in `MasterRenderSystem` directly would couple the renderer to the
334	transform; staging through `DrawComponent` keeps the renderer
335	agnostic.
336	**Breaks:** running `MeshPrepSystem` before `HierarchySystem` produces
337	meshes positioned by last frame's parent transform (one-frame lag on
338	parented meshes). Running it after `MasterRenderSystem` is too late —
339	the renderer uses the previous frame's world matrix.
340	**Tests:** none yet.
341	**Depends on:** foundation — "`HierarchySystem` must run ahead of any
342	system reading WorldPosition"; "Rendering systems run last in the
343	pipeline" (above).
344	
345	## `CompositeMeshGenerator` rebases indices into the combined buffer
346	
347	When `CompositeMeshGenerator.Generate()` walks its sub-generators, it
348	adds each sub-mesh's vertices to a combined vertex list and adds
349	`indexOffset` to each sub-mesh's indices before appending to the
350	combined index list. A sub-generator returning indices that already
351	reference the combined buffer's range would draw the wrong triangles.
352	
353	**Why:** composability is the design goal — a button outline + label
354	backdrop + glow can be one mesh entity. The rebase invariant is what
355	makes "just add another generator" work without per-generator
356	coordination.
357	**Breaks:** a custom generator that returns indices unrelated to its
358	own vertex buffer (e.g. via a stale cached array) corrupts the
359	composite's geometry. The bug manifests as visible triangles between
360	unrelated parts of the composite.
361	**Tests:** none yet.
362	**Depends on:** —
363	
364	## Open questions
365	
366	- **Same-Y flicker in practice** — has this surfaced? If so, the
367	  tiebreaker premise above needs to harden.
368	- **Mixed render targets per entity** — is it ever valid for the same
369	  entity to render on Main *and* HUD (via two separate `DrawComponent`s
370	  on different entities)? Probably always two entities, but not yet a
371	  settled convention.
372	- **`DrawElement` cache invalidation** — what happens if a prep system
373	  mutates `SpriteInfoComponent` after the draw queue was built?
374	- **Texturing meshes** — `MeshData` carries `VertexPositionColor`
375	  vertices; there's no `VertexPositionTexture` path. Whether to add one
376	  (and how it interacts with the SpriteBatch-based sprite path) is open.
377	- **Mesh culling extents** — meshes get `VisibleComponent` from
378	  `CullingSystem` based on `TransformComponent.WorldPosition` against
379	  the camera bounds. A mesh's actual extents (computed from its
380	  vertices) might lie outside the position's frustum, causing visible
381	  pop-out at edges. No bounding-box-from-vertices logic exists today.
382	
383	## Aspirational direction
384	
385	- `VisibleComponent` becomes a property of `DrawComponent` (removes the
386	  easy-to-miss tag).
387	- Multi-view (minimap / splitscreen / CCTV / portals) is now possible by
388	  composing `MasterRenderSystem` instances + `RenderLayer`s (the camera
389	  demo ships a minimap). What's still missing is **per-view culling**: a

391	  second camera can't yet cull to *its own* frustum. A per-camera cull set
392	  (or a cull-independent draw set option) is the next step.
393	- Render targets become more configurable — custom post-processing
394	  passes, shader effects.
395	- A `MeshTransformBatcher` that combines static meshes sharing a layer
396	  depth into a single submission, cutting `BasicEffect` draw calls.
397	- Per-vertex texture-coordinate support so meshes can sample sprite
398	  atlases (would let the dialogue indicator or UI nine-patches be a
399	  mesh rather than a `SpriteBatch` ninepatch).
400	
401	## Follow-up debt
402	
403	The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:
404	
405	- `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive
406	- `DrawComponent` is the only render component
407	- `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*
408	- One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass
409	- A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination
410	- `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list
411	- Renderable entity stack on the Main target
412	- `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`
413	- Three render targets, two behaviors
414	- `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp
415	- Rendering systems run last in the pipeline
416	- Layer-depth ownership pipeline
417	- Y-sort tiebreaker is parent-child bias only
418	- `Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable
419	- `IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list
420	- `MeshPrepSystem` writes the world matrix once per frame
421	- `CompositeMeshGenerator` rebases indices into the combined buffer

424	no game `SpriteBatch` calls, `VisibleComponent` not added outside

426	candidates here.

# rendering — premises

> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the rendering pipeline:
> `DrawComponent`, `SpriteInfoComponent`, `VisibleComponent`, the
> `Camera` class, render targets, `CullingSystem`, `SpritePrepSystem`,
> `YSortSystem`, `MasterRenderSystem`, `FinalDrawSystem`, plus the mesh
> primitives (`IMeshGenerator`, `MeshData`, `MeshPrepSystem`). Read this
> before changing any of those pieces or any system that produces draw
> data downstream.

## `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive

A `DrawComponent`'s `Type` is one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or
`Mesh`. One render component per renderable entity; an entity that needs
two visual types needs two entities (or a new `DrawElementType` that
composes both).

**Why:** `MasterRenderSystem` switches batch context based on `Type`
(`Sprite`/`Text`/`NinePatch` go through `SpriteBatch`, `Mesh` goes
through `BasicEffect` triangles). Allowing a single `DrawComponent` to
span two types would force every render path through a per-call branch.
**Breaks:** game code that sets a `DrawComponent` to one type and then
expects sprite + text behavior renders only one of them, with no
diagnostic.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `DrawComponent` is the only render component

Do not create new draw or render components. Adding a new visual type
extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork the
pipeline.

**Why:** a parallel render component would also need a parallel render
system, parallel culling treatment, and parallel layer-depth handling —
the framework's value comes from there being exactly one path through
the pipeline.
**Breaks:** the parallel system either skips entities the main path
expected (silent invisibility) or competes with it (z-fighting,
double-rendering).
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*

All `SpriteBatch` / `BasicEffect` draw calls happen inside
`MasterRenderSystem` (back-buffer composition is `FinalDrawSystem`'s job).
Game code must not call `SpriteBatch` directly and must not write a second
render system. This is about a single *implementation*, not a single
*instance*: a screen registers as many `MasterRenderSystem` instances as it
has views (see "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass").

**Why:** centralizing the draw call lets one well-understood class own the
render-target switch, the batch settings, the sort, and the layer-depth
contract. A bespoke second renderer fragments all four; N instances of the
*same* renderer do not.
**Breaks:** a parallel hand-rolled renderer fights over the active
`SpriteBatch`, producing flickering frames, dropped draws, or driver-level
errors, and bypasses the sort/layer-depth contract.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass

A `MasterRenderSystem` instance renders exactly one pass: every entity
whose `DrawComponent.Target` equals its `source` id, through its optional
`camera` (null ⇒ screen-space, identity transform), into its `destination`
render target, which it clears to transparent first. The `source == Main`
pass additionally filters on `VisibleComponent` (culling); screen-space
passes always render. Multiple cameras, minimaps, splitscreen, CCTV, and
portal textures are all just additional instances — a minimap is a second
instance with `source = Main`, a second camera, and its own target.
`FinalDrawSystem` then composites the targets onto the screen.

**Why:** decoupling *what* to draw (`source`), *how* (`camera`), and
*where* (`destination`) makes a second view a second instance, not a new
code path — the framework's general-over-specialized rule. It also removes
the old "the camera only applies to the Main-keyed target" coupling.
**Breaks:** two instances writing the *same* destination clear each
other's work (each clears on entry) — give every pass its own target and
let `FinalDrawSystem` overlap them. Expecting a non-Main source to honor
culling: only `source == Main` consults `VisibleComponent`.
**Tests:** none yet (the multi-pass + minimap path is exercised by the
camera demo, `MonoDreams/camera/demo/CameraDemoScreen.cs`).
**Depends on:** "A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its
destination".

## A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination

A `MasterRenderSystem` pass derives its mesh `BasicEffect` projection from
the *destination* render target's pixel size
(`CreateOrthographicOffCenter(0, dest.Width, dest.Height, 0, …)`), and the
camera's view transform centers the view at the camera's virtual
resolution. For the two to agree, a pass's `camera.VirtualWidth/Height`
must equal its destination render target's size. The minimap obeys this by
giving its second camera the same virtual resolution as the main camera and
a full-virtual-resolution target, then letting `FinalDrawSystem` shrink
that target into the on-screen box.

**Why:** projection maps destination pixels → NDC; the camera centers world
content at `(VirtualWidth/2, VirtualHeight/2)`. A mismatch puts the centered
content somewhere other than the target's middle and scales meshes wrongly.
Deriving projection from the destination (not the camera) is what lets
screen-space passes carry no camera at all.
**Breaks:** a camera whose virtual resolution differs from its destination
renders off-center and mis-scaled in that pass.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** "`Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable".

## `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list

`FinalDrawSystem` takes an ordered `RenderLayer` list and draws each
target onto the back buffer in order (later = on top). `RenderLayer.Main`
/ `UI` / `HUD` are factories for the standard full-frame layers (carrying
the viewport-mode-aware destination rect + sampler); `RenderLayer.Overlay`
places a target in a sub-rectangle given in HUD virtual coordinates,
mapped to the screen the same way the HUD layer is — so an overlay aligns
with HUD chrome drawn at those coordinates. The screen owns the list, so it
decides which targets exist, their order, and where each lands.

**Why:** the compositor is the natural seam for screen layout — overlays
(minimap, CCTV), and eventually tiled splitscreen — without touching the
renderer. Driving it from an explicit list (rather than a hardcoded
Main→UI→HUD sequence) makes those layouts data, not code forks.
**Breaks:** omitting a layer silently drops that target from the screen
(its render pass still ran and cleared its target — wasted work, blank
result). An overlay rect given in screen pixels instead of HUD virtual
coords misaligns with HUD chrome under non-1:1 scaling.
**Tests:** none yet (exercised by every demo/example screen and the minimap
overlay in the camera demo).
**Depends on:** —

## Renderable entity stack on the Main target

An entity is rendered to the Main target only if it has
`TransformComponent + SpriteInfoComponent (or text/mesh equivalent) +
DrawComponent + VisibleComponent`. Missing `VisibleComponent` means
`MasterRenderSystem` skips silently (it includes `.With<VisibleComponent>()`
in the Main-target query).

**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is the culling output. `CullingSystem` adds
it for entities inside the camera frustum and removes it for entities
outside, letting `MasterRenderSystem` skip a frustum check per entity.
Splitting it from `DrawComponent` is a wart — see Aspirational.
**Breaks:** the canonical missed-tag bug — a dev creates an entity with
`SpriteInfoComponent + DrawComponent` and stares at an invisible result
with no error. Forgetting to register `CullingSystem` in a new screen
makes everything Main-target invisible.
**Tests:** none yet. *This is the specific bug from the bootstrap
interview that motivated writing premises files in the first place.*
**Depends on:** "`VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`".

## `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`

Game code must not add or remove `VisibleComponent` on Main-target
entities. It is managed automatically by `CullingSystem` based on the
camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. UI and HUD entities may set
`VisibleComponent` themselves as a one-shot tag, since those targets
ignore culling (see "Three render targets, two behaviors").

**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is a derived state on the Main target. Manual
mutation creates ghost entities (visible but outside the frustum, wasting
draw calls) or phantom-invisible entities (inside the frustum but
skipped). `CullingSystem` will overwrite the game-set value next frame
anyway.
**Breaks:** entities flicker in and out as `CullingSystem` overwrites
game-set values frame to frame; or the cull check fights game code
forever.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Three render targets, two behaviors

`RenderTargetID.Main` is camera-transformed and respects culling.
`RenderTargetID.UI` and `RenderTargetID.HUD` are screen-space and always
render. Only Main consults `VisibleComponent`.

**Why:** UI and HUD are always-on-screen by definition. Culling them
would mean checking against the *screen* frustum, which is a degenerate
case (everything is inside). `MasterRenderSystem` enforces this by only
adding `.With<VisibleComponent>()` to the Main-target query.
**Breaks:** putting a Main-target entity on UI/HUD by mistake skips
camera transforms — the entity renders at its world coordinates,
unscaled by zoom. The reverse (UI on Main) gets culled away when the
camera moves.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp

`MasterRenderSystem` opens a separate `SpriteBatch` for sprites and for text so each gets
its own `SamplerState`. Sprites (and the mesh path) default to `PointClamp` — crisp
nearest-neighbour scaling for pixel art; text defaults to `LinearClamp` — smooth filtering
for bitmap fonts drawn at fractional scale. Both defaults are overridable via the
`spriteSampler` / `textSampler` constructor parameters. Because Sprite and Text are now
distinct batch types, the interleaved renderer flushes + reopens the batch when switching
between them; painter's order is preserved because the draw list is already depth-sorted.

**Why:** a single global `LinearClamp` blurred up-scaled pixel sprites (e.g. a 16×16
indicator drawn at 48×48); a single global `PointClamp` aliases down-scaled bitmap text.
Per-type samplers give each its correct filtering. The mesh path already forced `PointClamp`
(`ResetGraphicsStateForMeshRendering`), so sprites now match it.
**Breaks:** collapsing the Sprite/Text batch split (one sampler for both) forces a single
filter and reintroduces either blurry sprites or aliased text. Passing a non-clamp address
mode would wrap/tile sprites at their edges.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## The draw set is built once per instance, not per frame

A `MasterRenderSystem` instance builds its `EntitySet` (for its `source`)

**Breaks:** process memory climbs steadily even on a fully static scene

**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`
asserts a flat live heap across 600 frames of the camera demo (now four

**Depends on:** —

**Depends on:** —

  tiebreaker premise above needs to harden.
- **Mixed render targets per entity** — is it ever valid for the same
  entity to render on Main *and* HUD (via two separate `DrawComponent`s
  on different entities)? Probably always two entities, but not yet a
  settled convention.
- **`DrawElement` cache invalidation** — what happens if a prep system
  mutates `SpriteInfoComponent` after the draw queue was built?
- **Texturing meshes** — `MeshData` carries `VertexPositionColor`
  vertices; there's no `VertexPositionTexture` path. Whether to add one
  (and how it interacts with the SpriteBatch-based sprite path) is open.
- **Mesh culling extents** — meshes get `VisibleComponent` from
  `CullingSystem` based on `TransformComponent.WorldPosition` against
  the camera bounds. A mesh's actual extents (computed from its
  vertices) might lie outside the position's frustum, causing visible
  pop-out at edges. No bounding-box-from-vertices logic exists today.

## Aspirational direction

- `VisibleComponent` becomes a property of `DrawComponent` (removes the
  easy-to-miss tag).
- Multi-view (minimap / splitscreen / CCTV / portals) is now possible by
  composing `MasterRenderSystem` instances + `RenderLayer`s (the camera
  demo ships a minimap). What's still missing is **per-view culling**: a
  `source = Main` pass inherits the main camera's `VisibleComponent`, so a
  second camera can't yet cull to *its own* frustum. A per-camera cull set
  (or a cull-independent draw set option) is the next step.
- Render targets become more configurable — custom post-processing
  passes, shader effects.
- A `MeshTransformBatcher` that combines static meshes sharing a layer
  depth into a single submission, cutting `BasicEffect` draw calls.
- Per-vertex texture-coordinate support so meshes can sample sprite
  atlases (would let the dialogue indicator or UI nine-patches be a
  mesh rather than a `SpriteBatch` ninepatch).

## Follow-up debt

The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:

- `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive
- `DrawComponent` is the only render component
- `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*
- One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass
- A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination
- `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list
- Renderable entity stack on the Main target
- `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`
- Three render targets, two behaviors
- `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp
- Rendering systems run last in the pipeline
- Layer-depth ownership pipeline
- Y-sort tiebreaker is parent-child bias only
- `Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable
- `IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list
- `MeshPrepSystem` writes the world matrix once per frame
- `CompositeMeshGenerator` rebases indices into the combined buffer

Architectural tests for ECS-purity premises (no parallel render systems,
no game `SpriteBatch` calls, `VisibleComponent` not added outside
`CullingSystem` on Main-target entities) are the highest-leverage
candidates here.

All six changes are in and the full solution builds clean (`Compilação com êxito`, 0 errors). `HeadlessDemoTests` doesn't touch the physics screen, so nothing there is affected.

## What I changed

**`MonoDreams/physics/demo/PhysicsDemoScreen.cs`**
1. **Balls half size** — `MinBallRadius` 10→5, `MaxBallRadius` 20→10.
2. **Shorter header** — the 5-line description is now 2 lines: *"Balls bounce inside the box under gravity. / Red balls collide with each other; blue balls don't."*
3. **Brighter ball↔ball blink, independent of who/speed** — when two balls collide, **both** now blink a bright near-white pop (`BallCollisionFlashColor`), no longer gated by closing speed or by which ball is the message's base entity. Wall hits keep each ball's own vivid tint (still speed-gated so floor-resting balls don't stay lit). To keep wall and ball-collision colors from bleeding into each other, I added a `Flash(entity, color)` overload and centralized the per-ball colors in a `BallColors(type)` helper.
4. **Less energy lost per collision** — `Restitution` 0.85→0.92 (the live constant in `BallBounceSystem`, plus the matching screen-level constant).
5. **Inputs accept up to 999999** — `MaxBallsPerColor` 30→999999, input `maxLength` 2→6, and the number box is now auto-sized from the font so all six 9s fit without overflowing the border.
6. **Hollow blue balls** — blue balls now render with a new outline mesh (red stay solid). Their collider is unchanged — only the visual is hollow.

**`MonoDreams/rendering/Draw/IMeshGenerator.cs`** — added `CircleOutlineMeshGenerator` (the circular analog of `RectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`; emits a triangle list like the others). Updated the rendering premise that enumerates the canonical generators, and the demo's class docstring.

## Verification
Built and ran the headless self-verify path (`--screen physics`). The spawn frame confirms all six: 7 small solid red + 3 small hollow blue balls, the 2-line header, and the count inputs — all contained at spawn.

## One caveat worth knowing
While verifying, I found the physics box **empties out over a second or two in headless mode** — balls tunnel through the walls. I confirmed this is **pre-existing and not caused by the size change**: restoring the original 10–20px radius empties the box just as fast. The cause is that the headless host runs an *unclamped variable timestep* (`IsFixedTimeStep = false`), so its dt spikes (the first frame alone is ~0.3s, and each screenshot-save stalls the next frame) move balls hundreds of px in a single step — and ball↔wall collision is discrete SAT (only Box-vs-Box is swept). The **interactive** host runs a fixed 60fps timestep (≤17.5px/frame, well under the ~30px wall detection band), so containment holds there. I left this alone since it's an engine/host-level issue orthogonal to your six tweaks — but flagging it so an empty box in a headless run doesn't look like a regression.

any Transform-shaped contract — so a developer can swap in
`MyTransform` without re-implementing collision. The framework
doesn't enforce this today; the coupling is named here so the gap is
visible.
**Breaks:** a developer with `MyTransform` has to fork the collision
stack. The framework can't honestly call itself plug'n'play for
spatial substitutes until this loosens.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** foundation — "Don't mix two Transform-shaped components
in one project".

## `CollisionMessage` is the contract between detection and consumers

Detection emits `CollisionMessage` (or a custom message that satisfies
`ICollisionMessage` — `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is generic on
the message type via a `CreateCollisionMessageDelegate`). The message
carries the entity pair, contact point, contact normal, contact time,
penetration depth, layer, and collision type. Resolution systems and
game systems are the consumers.

**Why:** the generic message type lets games extend with custom fields
(damage, knockback strength, sound cue ID) without modifying the
framework. The base fields are the minimum contract for any contact.
**Breaks:** a custom message that drops a base field silently breaks
the resolution systems' assumption about what's available.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Known limitations (acknowledged gaps)

- **Tunneling at very high velocity** — swept collision prevents most
  tunneling, but at sufficiently extreme speed-to-collider-size
  ratios it can still occur. The only mitigation today is keeping
  gameplay velocities and collider sizes reasonable. *Velocity-cap
  safety net is on the backlog.*

## Open questions

- **`Passive` flag on `BoxColliderComponent` / `ConvexColliderComponent`** —
  the field exists but the semantic isn't yet documented (probably
  "detect but don't apply response"). Needs confirmation.
- **`ColliderTagComponent` on disposal** — is it auto-removed when the
  collider is removed, or only auto-added?

## Aspirational direction

- Loose coupling to `TransformComponent` so the collision stack works
  against any Transform-shaped contract.
- Multi-collider entities, if the use case appears — needs a defined
  combination semantic (intersection? union? per-layer override?).
- Velocity-cap safety net to prevent tunneling regardless of gameplay
  speed.

## Follow-up debt

The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:

- `ColliderTagComponent` is the canonical query target
- Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`
- Reference physics pipeline order
- `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design
- One collider of each type per entity
- Layer-based filtering is a coarse first filter
- Collision today couples to `TransformComponent` directly
- `CollisionMessage` is the contract between detection and consumers

The `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB` premise is the only one
with test protection. The pipeline-order premise is the highest-leverage
gap — an architectural test would catch screens that omit
`TransformCommitSystem`.

content.text:
I've got a definitive picture. Here's my assessment.

## The bottleneck is real and algorithmic: O(n²) broadphase

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem.Update` is a nested loop — every active collider (`_activeSet`) against every other collider (`_targets`):

```
foreach entity in all colliders (n):
    foreach target in all colliders (n):
        GetCollider + SharesLayerWith + build 2 AABBs + Intersects  → maybe SAT
```

At 360 red balls (+ blues + 4 walls ≈ 364 colliders) that's **~132,000 pair iterations every frame**, and it grows quadratically — double the balls, quadruple the work. Your "~360" stutter threshold is exactly where n² crosses the frame budget. Worse for *red* specifically: all reds share layer 0, so every red-red pair passes the layer filter and runs the per-pair work. The SAT narrowphase is already AABB-gated (cheap pairs reject early), so the cost is the sheer number of iterations, not the SAT math. The module's own premises even acknowledge this: *"without a layer cut, every entity tests against every other — O(n²) detection."*

Resolution is **not** the bottleneck — `BallBounceSystem` is O(collisions), linear.

## There's one genuinely good, non-speculative fix

**A spatial broadphase (uniform grid / spatial hash).** Bucket each collider's AABB into grid cells; only test pairs that share a cell. For many small, roughly-uniform colliders this turns the pair enumeration from O(n²) into ~O(n) — at 360 balls I'd expect on the order of **10–30× fewer broadphase iterations**, and the gap widens as you add more. This is the textbook solution for "many colliders," not a speculative micro-opt, and it directly answers your question. It can be **behavior-preserving**: same `CollisionMessage`s emitted, just without the wasted tests.

Caveats I'd handle in the implementation (all known invariants):
- Expand each dynamic collider's AABB by `Transform.Delta` before bucketing, so the swept Box-vs-Box path still can't tunnel (collision premise: *"swept collision reads Delta"*).
- Large/static colliders (the 4 walls span many cells) — insert into all overlapping cells, or test the handful of static colliders separately. Either is fine.
- Rebuild the grid each frame (O(n), cheap vs. what it saves); stays single-threaded (premise).

## Secondary wins exist but are diminishing without the grid

These are real but only constant-factor (~1.5–3× total, no change to the quadratic curve), so on their own they'd just nudge the stutter threshold:
- Cache the collider ref + box/convex flag once per outer entity instead of re-`GetCollider`/`Has` in the inner loop.
- Kill the `SharedLayers` LINQ `Intersect` allocation per collision.
- Dirty-flag static colliders to skip `UpdateWorldVertices` (there's already a `// TODO` for it) — tiny here (only 4 static walls).

And one tempting-but-not-free option: testing each unordered pair once (i<j) would halve the work, **but** your `BallBounceSystem` deliberately relies on receiving *both* (A,B) and (B,A) messages for its half-push symmetric resolution — so that change isn't free, it'd require rewriting resolution too.

## Scope note

This is the engine's shared collision system — the change benefits all three example games, touches the `collision` module's premises (I'd update the "layers are the only coarse filter" framing and add a broadphase test), and I'd run `SATCollisionTests` + `InfiniteRunnerTests` to confirm no regression. So it's a real framework change, which is why I want to confirm before building it.

## Layer-based filtering is a coarse first filter

Colliders with non-overlapping `ActiveLayers` sets are never tested
against each other. Layer membership is a fast first filter that
gameplay code uses to express groupings like "player vs world",
"player vs enemy", "projectiles vs everything".

**Why:** without a layer cut, every entity tests against every other
entity — O(n²) detection. Layers reduce that to O(n²) within each
layer pair.
**Breaks:** a missing layer membership makes two colliders silently
not collide — the dev tunes the game logic for hours before realizing
the layer wasn't set.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —
input.new_string:
## Layer-based filtering is the semantic pair filter

Colliders with non-overlapping `ActiveLayers` sets are never tested
against each other. Layer membership is the "should these ever collide?"
filter that gameplay code uses to express groupings like "player vs
world", "player vs enemy", "projectiles vs everything".

**Why:** layers express intent, not geometry. They are applied per
candidate pair *after* the spatial-grid broadphase has narrowed the
field by position (see "Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid"); together
they keep detection near O(n) for evenly distributed colliders rather
than all-pairs O(n²).
**Breaks:** a missing layer membership makes two colliders silently
not collide — the dev tunes the game logic for hours before realizing
the layer wasn't set.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** "Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid".

## Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid, and it is behavior-preserving

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` narrows candidate pairs with a
uniform spatial grid rebuilt every frame, not an all-pairs sweep. Each
enabled collider's world AABB — **expanded by its
`TransformComponent.Delta`** — is bucketed into every grid cell it
overlaps, and only colliders sharing a cell are pair-tested (deduped on
the *ordered* pair). The grid changes performance, not results: it emits
exactly the `CollisionMessage` set the old all-pairs loop did. Two
properties make that hold: (1) inserting into *all* overlapping cells
means any two colliders whose AABBs overlap always share a cell, so no
real contact is pruned; (2) expanding by `Delta` means a fast mover
shares a cell with anything along its swept path, so the swept
box-vs-box test is never starved. The dedup key is ordered — (A,B) and
(B,A) stay distinct — so the symmetric double-message that resolution may
rely on is preserved.

**Why:** all-pairs detection is O(n²) and stutters in the low hundreds of
colliders; the grid is ~O(n) for evenly distributed colliders (measured
~6× faster at 360 balls in the physics demo, and the gap widens with
count). Cell size adapts to the average collider AABB so small colliders
occupy ~one cell while the few large ones span several.
**Breaks:** bucketing by the un-expanded AABB lets a fast collider tunnel
(its swept path leaves the cells it was bucketed into) — the swept box
test silently misses contacts. Deduping on the *unordered* pair drops one
of the two symmetric messages, halving the impulse for resolvers that
expect both. Inserting into only one cell (e.g. the min-corner cell)
prunes real contacts whose colliders straddle a cell boundary.
**Tests:** behavior parity is covered indirectly — `SATCollisionTests`,
`InfiniteRunnerTests`, and `HeadlessDemoTests` pass unchanged after the
grid replaced the all-pairs loop.
**Depends on:** "Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`";
"`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design".

# collision — premises

> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the collision module:
> `BoxColliderComponent`, `ConvexColliderComponent`, `ColliderTagComponent`,
> `IColliderComponent`, `CollisionMessage`, `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`,
> and the two resolution systems. Read this before changing any of those
> pieces or any system that emits or consumes `CollisionMessage`.

## `ColliderTagComponent` is the canonical query target

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` queries entities by
`ColliderTagComponent`, not by `BoxColliderComponent` or
`ConvexColliderComponent`. The tag is auto-applied to any entity that
gains either collider component.

**Why:** the unification lets detection treat box and convex colliders
through the same query, dispatching to the right narrowphase test by
type at iteration time. Two separate queries would duplicate the
broadphase loop.
**Breaks:** game code that adds `ColliderTagComponent` manually (or
removes it while a collider remains) desyncs the tag from collider
presence — the entity is queried but has no collider to test, or has a
collider detection ignores.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`

Dynamic collision tests (e.g., `DynamicRectVsRect`,
`DynamicConvexVsConvex` in `SATCollision`) read
`TransformComponent.Delta` to compute the entity's movement vector.
Correct `Delta` requires `TransformCommitSystem` ran for the previous
frame.

**Why:** swept tests prevent tunneling — they check whether the movement
segment crosses the other collider, not just whether the endpoints
overlap.
**Breaks:** with a missing or stale `Delta`, fast-moving entities pass
through colliders. The bug is silent (no exception) and intermittent
(depends on speed).
**Tests:** none yet (the SAT primitives in
`MonoDreams.Tests/Collision/SATCollisionTests.cs` exercise the
narrowphase without going through a Delta-driven swept test).
**Depends on:** foundation — "`TransformComponent.Delta` is meaningful
only after `TransformCommitSystem` ran".

## `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB` must be refreshed when vertices change

Detection's broadphase filters on `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB`.
If the world vertices change (entity moved or rotated) without the AABB
being refreshed, the broadphase rejects an entity pair whose real
geometry would overlap.

**Why:** the broadphase is an early-exit fast filter. Out-of-date AABBs
defeat the filter's purpose by producing false negatives instead of
false positives.
**Breaks:** a real collision is invisible to the broadphase and never
reaches the narrowphase — entities silently pass through each other
even though their actual shapes overlap.
**Tests:**
`MonoDreams.Tests/Collision/SATCollisionTests.cs::ConvexCollider_BroadPhaseAABB_UpdatedAfterTransform`
verifies the detection system's own update path keeps the AABB fresh.
A custom system that mutates vertices outside detection has no
protection.
**Depends on:** —

## Reference physics pipeline order: Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit

Each stage owns one job and the next depends on the previous stage's
output. The screen's pipeline assembler is responsible for registering
these five stages in this order. Skipping or reordering them silently
degrades collision quality.

**Why:** Movement sets intent (game code writes `VelocityComponent`).
`VelocitySystem` applies intent to `TransformComponent.Position`.
`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` finds contacts using the new
position + the previous frame's `Delta`. Resolution corrects
positions/velocities to honor contacts. `TransformCommitSystem` closes
the frame so next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
**Breaks:** skip Commit → next frame's swept collision tunnels. Move
Resolution before Detection → resolution corrects against a stale
contact set. Mix gameplay position-writes with `VelocitySystem` → see
"`VelocitySystem` is the primary mover" in the physics module.
**Tests:** none yet (the integration tests exercise this order
implicitly —
`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/InfiniteRunnerTests.cs::PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`
depends on the full chain).
**Depends on:** physics — "`VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of
physics entities"; foundation — "`TransformComponent.Delta` is
meaningful only after `TransformCommitSystem` ran".

## `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design

The detection system holds instance-level polygon buffers
(`_boxPolyBufA`, `_boxPolyBufB`). It is not thread-safe; only one
instance should be registered and invoked at a time.

**Why:** the polygon buffers avoid per-collision allocations in the hot
path. Making them thread-local would re-introduce allocation pressure or
require an explicit pool.
**Breaks:** parallel invocations corrupt the buffers, producing nonsense
intersection tests — false positives, false negatives, or NaN-cascaded
entity positions.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## One collider of each type per entity

The framework assumes an entity has at most one `BoxColliderComponent`
and at most one `ConvexColliderComponent`. Multiple colliders of the
same type on a single entity is undefined behavior.

**Why:** the assumption simplifies queries and narrowphase dispatch.
The use case for multi-collider entities (e.g., one body, multiple
hitboxes) hasn't appeared, so the framework hasn't designed for it.
**Breaks:** queries pick one collider non-deterministically; detection
may test against the wrong one. If the use case appears, this becomes
a framework change, not a workaround.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Layer-based filtering is a coarse first filter

Colliders with non-overlapping `ActiveLayers` sets are never tested
against each other. Layer membership is a fast first filter that
gameplay code uses to express groupings like "player vs world",
"player vs enemy", "projectiles vs everything".

**Why:** without a layer cut, every entity tests against every other
entity — O(n²) detection. Layers reduce that to O(n²) within each
layer pair.
**Breaks:** a missing layer membership makes two colliders silently
not collide — the dev tunes the game logic for hours before realizing
the layer wasn't set.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Collision today couples to `TransformComponent` directly

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` and the resolution systems read
`TransformComponent` by type — `TransformComponent.Position`,
`TransformComponent.Delta`, and `ConvexColliderComponent.WorldVertices`
(refreshed from `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix`). *Status:
implementation debt.*

**Why:** the eventual end-state is loose coupling — collision against
any Transform-shaped contract — so a developer can swap in
`MyTransform` without re-implementing collision. The framework
doesn't enforce this today; the coupling is named here so the gap is
visible.
**Breaks:** a developer with `MyTransform` has to fork the collision
stack. The framework can't honestly call itself plug'n'play for
spatial substitutes until this loosens.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** foundation — "Don't mix two Transform-shaped components
in one project".

## `CollisionMessage` is the contract between detection and consumers

Detection emits `CollisionMessage` (or a custom message that satisfies
`ICollisionMessage` — `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is generic on
the message type via a `CreateCollisionMessageDelegate`). The message
carries the entity pair, contact point, contact normal, contact time,
penetration depth, layer, and collision type. Resolution systems and
game systems are the consumers.

**Why:** the generic message type lets games extend with custom fields
(damage, knockback strength, sound cue ID) without modifying the
framework. The base fields are the minimum contract for any contact.
**Breaks:** a custom message that drops a base field silently breaks
the resolution systems' assumption about what's available.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Known limitations (acknowledged gaps)

- **Tunneling at very high velocity** — swept collision prevents most
  tunneling, but at sufficiently extreme speed-to-collider-size
  ratios it can still occur. The only mitigation today is keeping
  gameplay velocities and collider sizes reasonable. *Velocity-cap
  safety net is on the backlog.*

## Open questions

- **`Passive` flag on `BoxColliderComponent` / `ConvexColliderComponent`** —
  the field exists but the semantic isn't yet documented (probably
  "detect but don't apply response"). Needs confirmation.
- **`ColliderTagComponent` on disposal** — is it auto-removed when the
  collider is removed, or only auto-added?

## Aspirational direction

- Loose coupling to `TransformComponent` so the collision stack works
  against any Transform-shaped contract.
- Multi-collider entities, if the use case appears — needs a defined
  combination semantic (intersection? union? per-layer override?).
- Velocity-cap safety net to prevent tunneling regardless of gameplay
  speed.

## Follow-up debt

The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:

- `ColliderTagComponent` is the canonical query target
- Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`
- Reference physics pipeline order
- `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design

The `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB` premise is the only one
with test protection. The pipeline-order premise is the highest-leverage
gap — an architectural test would catch screens that omit
`TransformCommitSystem`.

Done. Here's the collision optimization.

## What was wrong
`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` ran an **all-pairs O(n²) broadphase** — every collider against every other. At 360 same-layer red balls that's ~130k pair iterations/frame, and it quadruples each time you double the count, which is exactly why it cliff-edged around 360.

## What I changed
Replaced the nested loop in `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem.cs` with a **uniform spatial-grid broadphase**, rebuilt each frame:
- One O(n) pass snapshots each collider's world AABB (and refreshes convex world-vertices as before).
- Each collider is bucketed into every grid cell its AABB overlaps; only colliders sharing a cell get pair-tested.
- Cell size adapts to the average collider AABB, so small balls land in ~1 cell while the few big walls span several.
- All per-frame structures (entry list, cell lists, dedup set) are pooled/reused — no steady-state allocation.

It's **behavior-preserving** — same `CollisionMessage` set as before — and I was careful about the two things that would silently break that:
- **AABBs are expanded by `Transform.Delta`** before bucketing, so a fast mover still shares a cell with anything on its swept path (the box-vs-box test is swept — bucketing by the static AABB would reintroduce tunneling).
- **Dedup is on the *ordered* pair**, so the symmetric (A,B)+(B,A) double-message your `BallBounceSystem` relies on for its half-push is preserved.

## Measured impact
Benchmarked grid vs. the committed O(n²) version (stashed to get a clean baseline), 360 balls, 600 frames:

| Broadphase | Sim time | 
|---|---|
| O(n²) | 8.66 s |
| Grid | 1.36 s |

**~6× faster at 360**, and because it's ~O(n) vs O(n²), the headroom keeps growing as you add colliders.

- Full test suite: **32/32 pass unchanged** (includes `SATCollisionTests`, `InfiniteRunnerTests`, `HeadlessDemoTests` — the detection→resolution chain and the demos).
- Full solution builds clean.
- Updated `collision/docs/premises.md`: reframed the layer-filter premise (the old "layers reduce to O(n²)" line was now wrong) and added a **"Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid"** premise documenting the Delta-expansion and ordered-dedup invariants.

- **Halving work via unordered pairs** — would break your symmetric double-message resolution; not free.
- **`SharedLayers` LINQ allocation** — only fires on actual collisions, not the hot pair loop; minor.

# collision — premises

> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the collision module:
> `BoxColliderComponent`, `ConvexColliderComponent`, `ColliderTagComponent`,
> `IColliderComponent`, `CollisionMessage`, `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`,
> and the two resolution systems. Read this before changing any of those
> pieces or any system that emits or consumes `CollisionMessage`.

## `ColliderTagComponent` is the canonical query target

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` queries entities by
`ColliderTagComponent`, not by `BoxColliderComponent` or
`ConvexColliderComponent`. The tag is auto-applied to any entity that
gains either collider component.

**Why:** the unification lets detection treat box and convex colliders
through the same query, dispatching to the right narrowphase test by
type at iteration time. Two separate queries would duplicate the
broadphase loop.
**Breaks:** game code that adds `ColliderTagComponent` manually (or
removes it while a collider remains) desyncs the tag from collider
presence — the entity is queried but has no collider to test, or has a
collider detection ignores.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`

Dynamic collision tests (e.g., `DynamicRectVsRect`,
`DynamicConvexVsConvex` in `SATCollision`) read
`TransformComponent.Delta` to compute the entity's movement vector.
Correct `Delta` requires `TransformCommitSystem` ran for the previous
frame.

**Why:** swept tests prevent tunneling — they check whether the movement
segment crosses the other collider, not just whether the endpoints
overlap.
**Breaks:** with a missing or stale `Delta`, fast-moving entities pass
through colliders. The bug is silent (no exception) and intermittent
(depends on speed).
**Tests:** none yet (the SAT primitives in
`MonoDreams.Tests/Collision/SATCollisionTests.cs` exercise the
narrowphase without going through a Delta-driven swept test).
**Depends on:** foundation — "`TransformComponent.Delta` is meaningful
only after `TransformCommitSystem` ran".

## `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB` must be refreshed when vertices change

Detection's broadphase filters on `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB`.
If the world vertices change (entity moved or rotated) without the AABB
being refreshed, the broadphase rejects an entity pair whose real
geometry would overlap.

**Why:** the broadphase is an early-exit fast filter. Out-of-date AABBs
defeat the filter's purpose by producing false negatives instead of
false positives.
**Breaks:** a real collision is invisible to the broadphase and never
reaches the narrowphase — entities silently pass through each other
even though their actual shapes overlap.
**Tests:**
`MonoDreams.Tests/Collision/SATCollisionTests.cs::ConvexCollider_BroadPhaseAABB_UpdatedAfterTransform`
verifies the detection system's own update path keeps the AABB fresh.
A custom system that mutates vertices outside detection has no
protection.
**Depends on:** —

## Reference physics pipeline order: Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit

Each stage owns one job and the next depends on the previous stage's
output. The screen's pipeline assembler is responsible for registering
these five stages in this order. Skipping or reordering them silently
degrades collision quality.

**Why:** Movement sets intent (game code writes `VelocityComponent`).
`VelocitySystem` applies intent to `TransformComponent.Position`.
`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` finds contacts using the new
position + the previous frame's `Delta`. Resolution corrects
positions/velocities to honor contacts. `TransformCommitSystem` closes
the frame so next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
**Breaks:** skip Commit → next frame's swept collision tunnels. Move
Resolution before Detection → resolution corrects against a stale
contact set. Mix gameplay position-writes with `VelocitySystem` → see
"`VelocitySystem` is the primary mover" in the physics module.
**Tests:** none yet (the integration tests exercise this order
implicitly —
`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/InfiniteRunnerTests.cs::PlayerFallsOffLeftEdge`
depends on the full chain).
**Depends on:** physics — "`VelocitySystem` is the primary mover of
physics entities"; foundation — "`TransformComponent.Delta` is
meaningful only after `TransformCommitSystem` ran".

## `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design

The detection system holds instance-level polygon buffers
(`_boxPolyBufA`, `_boxPolyBufB`). It is not thread-safe; only one
instance should be registered and invoked at a time.

**Why:** the polygon buffers avoid per-collision allocations in the hot
path. Making them thread-local would re-introduce allocation pressure or
require an explicit pool.
**Breaks:** parallel invocations corrupt the buffers, producing nonsense
intersection tests — false positives, false negatives, or NaN-cascaded
entity positions.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## One collider of each type per entity

The framework assumes an entity has at most one `BoxColliderComponent`
and at most one `ConvexColliderComponent`. Multiple colliders of the
same type on a single entity is undefined behavior.

**Why:** the assumption simplifies queries and narrowphase dispatch.
The use case for multi-collider entities (e.g., one body, multiple
hitboxes) hasn't appeared, so the framework hasn't designed for it.
**Breaks:** queries pick one collider non-deterministically; detection
may test against the wrong one. If the use case appears, this becomes
a framework change, not a workaround.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Layer-based filtering is the semantic pair filter

Colliders with non-overlapping `ActiveLayers` sets are never tested
against each other. Layer membership is the "should these ever collide?"
filter that gameplay code uses to express groupings like "player vs
world", "player vs enemy", "projectiles vs everything".

**Why:** layers express intent, not geometry. They are applied per
candidate pair *after* the spatial-grid broadphase has narrowed the
field by position (see "Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid"); together
they keep detection near O(n) for evenly distributed colliders rather
than all-pairs O(n²).
**Breaks:** a missing layer membership makes two colliders silently
not collide — the dev tunes the game logic for hours before realizing
the layer wasn't set.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** "Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid".

## Broadphase is a uniform spatial grid, and it is behavior-preserving

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` narrows candidate pairs with a
uniform spatial grid rebuilt every frame, not an all-pairs sweep. Each
enabled collider's world AABB — **expanded by its
`TransformComponent.Delta`** — is bucketed into every grid cell it
overlaps, and only colliders sharing a cell are pair-tested (deduped on
the *ordered* pair). The grid changes performance, not results: it emits
exactly the `CollisionMessage` set the old all-pairs loop did. Two
properties make that hold: (1) inserting into *all* overlapping cells
means any two colliders whose AABBs overlap always share a cell, so no
real contact is pruned; (2) expanding by `Delta` means a fast mover
shares a cell with anything along its swept path, so the swept
box-vs-box test is never starved. The dedup key is ordered — (A,B) and
(B,A) stay distinct — so the symmetric double-message that resolution may
rely on is preserved.

**Why:** all-pairs detection is O(n²) and stutters in the low hundreds of
colliders; the grid is ~O(n) for evenly distributed colliders (measured
~6× faster at 360 balls in the physics demo, and the gap widens with
count). Cell size adapts to the average collider AABB so small colliders
occupy ~one cell while the few large ones span several.
**Breaks:** bucketing by the un-expanded AABB lets a fast collider tunnel
(its swept path leaves the cells it was bucketed into) — the swept box
test silently misses contacts. Deduping on the *unordered* pair drops one
of the two symmetric messages, halving the impulse for resolvers that
expect both. Inserting into only one cell (e.g. the min-corner cell)
prunes real contacts whose colliders straddle a cell boundary.
**Tests:** behavior parity is covered indirectly — `SATCollisionTests`,
`InfiniteRunnerTests`, and `HeadlessDemoTests` pass unchanged after the
grid replaced the all-pairs loop.
**Depends on:** "Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`";
"`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design".

## Collision today couples to `TransformComponent` directly

`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` and the resolution systems read
`TransformComponent` by type — `TransformComponent.Position`,
`TransformComponent.Delta`, and `ConvexColliderComponent.WorldVertices`
(refreshed from `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix`). *Status:
implementation debt.*

**Why:** the eventual end-state is loose coupling — collision against
any Transform-shaped contract — so a developer can swap in
`MyTransform` without re-implementing collision. The framework
doesn't enforce this today; the coupling is named here so the gap is
visible.
**Breaks:** a developer with `MyTransform` has to fork the collision
stack. The framework can't honestly call itself plug'n'play for
spatial substitutes until this loosens.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** foundation — "Don't mix two Transform-shaped components
in one project".

## `CollisionMessage` is the contract between detection and consumers

Detection emits `CollisionMessage` (or a custom message that satisfies
`ICollisionMessage` — `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is generic on
the message type via a `CreateCollisionMessageDelegate`). The message
carries the entity pair, contact point, contact normal, contact time,
penetration depth, layer, and collision type. Resolution systems and
game systems are the consumers.

**Why:** the generic message type lets games extend with custom fields
(damage, knockback strength, sound cue ID) without modifying the
framework. The base fields are the minimum contract for any contact.
**Breaks:** a custom message that drops a base field silently breaks
the resolution systems' assumption about what's available.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Known limitations (acknowledged gaps)

- **Tunneling at very high velocity** — swept collision prevents most
  tunneling, but at sufficiently extreme speed-to-collider-size
  ratios it can still occur. The only mitigation today is keeping
  gameplay velocities and collider sizes reasonable. *Velocity-cap
  safety net is on the backlog.*

## Open questions

- **`Passive` flag on `BoxColliderComponent` / `ConvexColliderComponent`** —
  the field exists but the semantic isn't yet documented (probably
  "detect but don't apply response"). Needs confirmation.
- **`ColliderTagComponent` on disposal** — is it auto-removed when the
  collider is removed, or only auto-added?

## Aspirational direction

- Loose coupling to `TransformComponent` so the collision stack works
  against any Transform-shaped contract.
- Multi-collider entities, if the use case appears — needs a defined
  combination semantic (intersection? union? per-layer override?).
- Velocity-cap safety net to prevent tunneling regardless of gameplay
  speed.

## Follow-up debt

The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:

- `ColliderTagComponent` is the canonical query target
- Swept collision reads `TransformComponent.Delta`
- Reference physics pipeline order
- `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` is single-threaded by design
- One collider of each type per entity
- Layer-based filtering is the semantic pair filter
- Collision today couples to `TransformComponent` directly
- `CollisionMessage` is the contract between detection and consumers

The `ConvexColliderComponent.BroadPhaseAABB` premise is the only one
with test protection. The pipeline-order premise is the highest-leverage
gap — an architectural test would catch screens that omit
`TransformCommitSystem`.

content.text:
I read the demo's custom resolver (`BallBounceSystem.Resolve`, `PhysicsDemoScreen.cs:810`). The jitter isn't a bug in the new grid broadphase — it's inherent to how this resolver handles *resting* contact. Here's the precise why.

## Why they never settle

Three things compound:

**1. No rest threshold + high restitution (0.92).** Every contact is treated as a *bouncy* collision. The reflection at `PhysicsDemoScreen.cs:854` is:

```
velocity.Current -= (1f + Restitution) * impactSpeed * normal;   // (1 + 0.92) = 1.92×
```

Gravity feeds `g·dt` ≈ `1200 × 1/60` ≈ **20 px/s of inward speed into the floor every frame**. The resolver reflects that back at ~92%, so a ball "sitting" on the floor actually gets kicked up ~38 px/s each frame, falls, and repeats. There is no closing-speed below which a contact is treated as *resting* (restitution 0) instead of *bouncing* — so a pile can never go quiet.

**2. Full, immediate positional correction with no slop.** `transform.Translate(-normal * penetration * pushScale)` (`:844`) shoves the ball *all the way* out of penetration that same frame. With many balls this is an over-constrained system solved by a single Gauss-Seidel pass in arbitrary message order: resolving A↔B shoves A into C; resolving A↔C shoves it back. One iteration per frame can't satisfy a packed stack, so positions shuffle every frame — that's the overlap shimmer you see.

**3. Nothing dissipates residual energy.** No friction, damping, or sleeping. Tiny velocities never die; cause (1) keeps re-amplifying them.

Net: there's no static equilibrium reachable, so the system lands in a noisy limit cycle. With **floor boost on** this *is* the intended perpetual-motion showcase (the class doc literally says "self-sustaining, not damped"). With boost **off** + many balls, the exact same machinery just reads as jitter.

## The graceful fix (recommended)

Two small, **velocity-gated** tweaks, both contained in the demo's `BallBounceSystem` — no engine contract change, and the energetic floor-boost-on behavior stays byte-for-byte identical because both only engage at low closing speed:

- **Rest/bounce threshold.** Below a small closing speed (a few × `g·dt`, ~30–60 px/s), treat the contact as resting: cancel *only* the inward normal velocity (`v -= impactSpeed·n`, i.e. restitution 0) instead of reflecting it. Above the threshold, bounce at 0.92 as today. This kills the perpetual micro-bounce — slow piles go still. (It's exactly the behavior the engine's own `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` uses; we'd just be blending: stop when slow, bounce when fast.)
- **Penetration slop + partial correction.** Ignore overlaps under a slop (~0.5 px) and correct only a fraction (~0.2–0.5) of the remainder per frame. Stops the position-fighting in dense piles; the sub-pixel residual overlap is invisible.

This is the standard "resting contact" recipe (it's what Box2D's velocity threshold + linear slop + Baumgarte do) and it directly targets both visible symptoms while leaving the showcase untouched.

## Heavier options (only if you want more)

- **Sleeping** — freeze a ball whose speed stays under a threshold for N frames, wake on contact. Best for genuine stillness *and* a real perf win at high counts, but it's more code and slightly against the "always alive" framing.
- **Global linear damping** — simplest, one line, but changes the feel everywhere and fights the "not damped" design intent.

My recommendation is the two gated tweaks — small, surgical, demo-local, and they leave floor-boost-on exactly as-is. Want me to implement them?

content.text:
All 32 tests pass, build is clean.

## What changed
All in the demo's `BallBounceSystem` (`PhysicsDemoScreen.cs`) — no engine contract touched:

1. **Rest/bounce threshold** (`RestThreshold = 50f`). A contact whose closing speed is below ~50 px/s (≈2.5× gravity's per-frame nudge) is treated as resting: restitution drops to `0`, so the resolver cancels *only* the inward normal velocity instead of reflecting it at 0.92. Tangential motion survives, so balls can still slide/roll into the pile. Above the threshold, the elastic bounce is byte-for-byte unchanged.

2. **Slop + partial positional correction** (`PenetrationSlop = 0.5f`, `PositionCorrection = 0.5f`). Overlaps under ½ px are ignored, and only half the remaining penetration is pushed out per frame. Packed neighbors no longer fully shove each other every frame, so the over-constrained stack relaxes instead of shimmering. Steady-state residual overlap works out to ~1 px — sub-pixel against radius 5–10 balls.
